---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: 张宝林 <robust...@foxmail.com>
Date: Wed, Mar 28, 2018 at 4:15 AM
Subject: Model conflict
To: "nickmatzke.ncse" <nickmat...@gmail.com>


Dear Nick,

I have another question about the models. As you can see the comparisons in the PPT and more clear figures in PDF files. We have used AIC weights to compared all six models in BioGeoBEARS, the best model is DEC+J with AIC_wt=0.87. Although with the highest AIC weight, I have some concerns with the DEC+J results because it shown strong conflicts with the other two methods (DIVA and BAYAREA):

1. Confict 1: as you can clear see in the ppt, the DEC+J strongly support a vicariance scenario, the ancestor is AC, then split to A and C. However, the DIVA and BAYAREA both strongly support a dispersal model, that is the ancestor from A area have descendant dispersal to C or leave in the same area A. I have no idea which one is right because they both make sense. In another words, we don't have strong evidence to reject each other scenario. Although the AIC weight can tell something but not everything. I think the best situation is all the methods support the same scenario, then we can tell the audiences something with more confidence.

2. In Confict 2.  Here is the place that make me more doubt about the DEC+J results. As you can see the descendants are one C and several F, according to the parsimony thought, the ancestor should be CF (at least). However, the real result in DEC+J for that node is C. That seems unbelieveable and make me doubt how does DEC+J can get result.

The package version of BioGeoBEARS I used is ‘0.2.1’.

Thanks for your time and help. Very appreciate that.

Best wishes,

Baolin

Hi -- briefly...


On Wed, Oct 18, 2017 at 12:35 AM, 张宝林 <robust...@foxmail.com> wrote:
Dear Nick,

Thanks for the quick reply.

Yes, as you said, the "areas allowed" setup is a different thing than dispersal multipliers. What I am think before maybe too simple. For example, the pairs where have 0.5 dispersal probility in dispersal multipliersin doesn't mean these two area have 0.5 possibility are allowed. It works when I change the value of 0.5 to 1 in "area allowed matrix".

Actually what I am trying to analyze is to compare two phylogeographical hypothese. One hypothsis allow some area can dispersal (M1), while another hypothsis not allowed (M2).  For each hypothsis, I add founder-event speciation (+j) and no j, respectively. Therefore, I have four scenarios: M1, M1+j, M2, M2+j in total.  But the problem is how to choose the best model? In many published papers,  they select the best model according the LnL or AIC value, but don't give statistical value. In may case, I found M1+j and M2+j both show good AIC values, 138.3 and 124.5 respectively. However, because I don't have statistical test, I'm not confident to say M2+j are significanlty better. I mentioned this becuase it is a long debated phylogeographical question. I'm afraid the reviewer may argue for this point. In the online script, I found you compare, eg. M1 and M1+j like this:
"
LnL_2 = get_LnL_from_BioGeoBEARS_results_object(resDEC)
LnL_1 = get_LnL_from_BioGeoBEARS_results_object(resDECj)

numparams1 = 3
numparams2 = 2
stats = AICstats_2models(LnL_1, LnL_2, numparams1, numparams2)
stats
"

This procedures will give pval using chi-squared method.



Actually, AICstats_2models gives you AICs, not p-values.

The chi-squared method is the likelihood ratio test (LRT).  This can compare only pairs of models, and only if they are nested:

See: http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#nesting

M1 is nested inside M1+j
M2 is nested inside M2+j

M1 is NOT nested inside M2 or M2+j
...etc...
 
Can I compare the M1+j and M2+j like this? I wonder this because M1 and M2 are based on different "dispersal multipliers matrix" and "area allowed matrix". It's a different thing than M1 and M1+j.


You should use AIC or AICc to compare non-nested models -- and, as a bonus, you can compare all of the models at once, as long as the trees and the geography ranges at the tips are the same between all of them.

AICs do not give you p-values. If a reviewer demands p-values, tell them they are out of date with modern statistics and that statistical model comparison with AIC is a standard method (well, don't tell them this, think it privately and say something more polite in your reply).  As I like to say:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#AIC_Bible
======================
The "Bible" of AIC/AICc is:

Burnham, Kenneth P.; Anderson, David R. (1998, first edition; 2002, second edition). Model Selection and Multimodel Inference: A Practical Information-Theoretic Approach. New York, Springer. doi: 10.1007/b97636
Link: http://www.springer.com/gb/book/9780387953649

I like to point out that it has 36,458 citations (as of 2017-04-18): https://scholar.google.com.au/scholar?hl=en&q=Burnham%2C+Kenneth+P.%2C+Anderson%2C+David+R.&btnG=&as_sdt=1%2C5&as_sdtp=

On occasion, I see reviewers or editors that are confused/ambivalent about AIC. Probably this is just due to unfamiliarity — entire generations of scientists were trained in nothing but traditional "frequentist" statistics, and the may get nervous if they do not see a P-value. In such situations, I recommend that authors respond by pointing out that AIC, AICc, etc. are now standard, well-known techniques in science, even if they are new in biogeography. A statistical method with 36,000+ citations should not need to be re-explained, from scratch, in every new scientific article using the method. Citation of Burnham and Anderson (2002) should be enough, and readers who are confused about AIC and related approaches should be referred to Burnham and Anderson (2002), and/or the references below.
======================


 
Nevertheness, this procedure don't show singnificant p value although M2+j are better accoding to AIC value. What I have done is meaningful?


The whole concept of "statistical significance" is actually a debatable part of a debatable statistical philosophy called "frequentism".  Don't get me wrong, frequentism and p-values can be useful, but they should not be blindly required when other well-known statistical procedures are available.

See the graphics in reference 12, here:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#refs

...for a way to think about model comparison in a continuous way, rather than significant/nonsignificant.

Cheers!
Nick


 

Thanks for you suggestions again. Quit help!

Best regards,

Baolin Zhang

Hi -- your files are working for me (when I take the example script at: http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script .. and modify it for your files).

Your issue may be this line in your script:

===============
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$dispersal_multipliers_fn = "dispersal_multipliers.txt"
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$areas_allowed_fn = "dispersal_multipliers.txt"
===============

I would change to:

===============
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$dispersal_multipliers_fn = "dispersal_multipliers.txt"
#BioGeoBEARS_run_object$areas_allowed_fn = "dispersal_multipliers.txt"
===============

The "areas allowed" setup is a different thing than dispersal multipliers, and probably not the best way to set up custom lists of ranges in each time period. 

See e.g.:

Areas-allowed matrix
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#areas_allowed_matrix2

Areas-adjacency matrix
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#areas_adjacency_matrix2

Manually modifying the list of states/ranges — A BETTER SOLUTION than the areas-adjacency matrix
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#better_than_adjacency

And other discussions:
https://www.google.com.au/search?q=areas+allowed+biogeobears&oq=areas+allowed+biogeobears&aqs=chrome..69i57.4759j0j7&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8


Also: setting

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$on_NaN_error = -1e50

...in the script (see http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script  ) will help with numerical problems during the optimization run, although not if you get a Nan Error on the first test likelihood calculation.

Working script and inputs attached.

Cheers,
Nick






On Mon, Oct 16, 2017 at 3:18 AM, 张宝林 <robust...@foxmail.com> wrote:
Dear Nick,

Firstly I would like to say sorry for I cannot post this information in google group. I think it is blocked in China.

I want to use BioGeoBEARS to run a constrained model with dispersal multipliers matrix in different time periods. Here I have upload the Rcode that I have used. However, I have got the following error message.
"
print(relative_probs_of_each_state_at_branch_top_AT_node_DOWNPASS[right_desc_nodenum,]):

 [1] NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN
Error in calc_loglike_sp(tip_condlikes_of_data_on_each_state = subtree_tip_relative_probs_of_each_state,  :
 

Stopping on error. This may mean your transition matrix disallows necessary transitions.  E.g., if your ranges are 'A' and 'B', and your model is DEC, then allowing range 'AB' as a possible state is required, so that you can get from 'A' to 'B' via 'AB' as the intermediate.
"

I have google the error message. Most of the answers say the error seems come from there are 0s in the dispersal matrix. However, the error remains after I have changed the 0s to 0.01. I can't figure it out for almost two weeks, so I have upload all the data that I used. Can you help me find out what happened? Thanks a lot. I really appreciate for that.

Best regards,

Baolin

Hi Baolin, some quick thoughts:
On Wed, Mar 28, 2018 at 4:15 AM, 张宝林 <robust...@foxmail.com> wrote:
Dear Nick,

I have another question about the models. As you can see the comparisons in the PPT and more clear figures in PDF files. We have used AIC weights to compared all six models in BioGeoBEARS, the best model is DEC+J with AIC_wt=0.87. Although with the highest AIC weight, I have some concerns with the DEC+J results because it shown strong conflicts with the other two methods (DIVA and BAYAREA):

1. Confict 1: as you can clear see in the ppt, the DEC+J strongly support a vicariance scenario, the ancestor is AC, then split to A and C.

Actually, DEC and DEC+J allow the "subset sympatry" scenario also, where at a node you can have a scenario like this: AC->AC,A.  See: 
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic


I think that, because this scenario is allowed in DEC and DEC+J, but not in DIVALIKE/DIVALIKE+J, or BAYAREALIKE/BAYAREALIKE+J, this makes "AC" a more probable ancestor at those nodes.  So really, this is not telling you that vicariance is more probable under DEC+J, it is saying that subset sympatry is more probable.

However, the DIVA and BAYAREA both strongly support a dispersal model, that is the ancestor from A area have descendant dispersal to C or leave in the same area A. I have no idea which one is right because they both make sense. In another words, we don't have strong evidence to reject each other scenario. Although the AIC weight can tell something but not everything. I think the best situation is all the methods support the same scenario, then we can tell the audiences something with more confidence.

I would disagree that it is "good" if all the methods support the same scenario!  Ideally, all the evidence/likelihood supports one model, and contradicts the rest of them!  Then, under a particular model, ideally one specific event history is supported, but often we aren't that lucky.  Note that even when DEC+J is very strongly supported, there are still a variety of specific historical scenarios that are possible, see Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping to visualize/measure the variability.  The pie charts are just a summary of this:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#stochastic_mapping

In your case, if AIC_wt is 0.87, this is what I would call "suggestive" evidence -- it is a little bit of evidence, not overwhelming evidence. See: 

Interpreting delta-AICs/differences in AIC: Some handy graphics from Burnham, Anderson, & Huyvaert (2011)
http://phylo.wikidot.com/advice-on-statistical-model-comparison-in-biogeobears#interpreting_deltaAICs


Also, note that "model" and "scenario"/"event"/"history" are different concepts.

2. In Confict 2.  Here is the place that make me more doubt about the DEC+J results. As you can see the descendants are one C and several F, according to the parsimony thought, the ancestor should be CF (at least). However, the real result in DEC+J for that node is C. That seems unbelieveable and make me doubt how does DEC+J can get result.

"Parsimony-thinking" can be hazardous in model-based biogeography:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#ace_not_arr

The information for estimating the range at a node comes not just from the nodes above, but also from the ancestor node (which conveys information from the rest of the tree). 

Because A/C are possible ancestor areas, this raises the probably of C over F at the node with Conflict 2.  Under DEC+J, the ancestral range is pretty confidently AC, with the daughters being pretty confidently AC and C, so DEC+J infers that the conflict-2-node was C, with a jump dispersal to F.

You can see that under DIVALIKE+J and BAYAREALIKE+J, that node is only about 60% in favor of "C", which is closer to your intuitions.
The package version of BioGeoBEARS I used is ‘0.2.1’.

Just make sure you sourced the updates, which fix a bug in the uppass range probabilities calculation, although the probabilities probably wouldn't change much either way:

http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#script
